prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Here lies, whom hound did ne’er pursue, Nor swifter greyhound follow, Whose foot ne’er tainted morning dew, Nor ear heard huntsman’s hallo’, Old Tiney, surliest of his kind, Who, nursed with tender care, And to domesticate bounds confined, Was still a wild jack-hare. Though duly from my hand he took His pittance every night, He did it with a jealous look, And, when he could, would bite. His diet was of wheaten bread, And milk, and oats, and straw, Thistles, or lettuces instead, With sand to scour his maw. On twigs of hawthorn he regaled, On pippins’ russet peel; And, when his juicy salads failed, Sliced carrot pleased him well. A Turkey carpet was his lawn, Whereon he loved to bound, To skip and gambol like a fawn, And swing his rump around. His frisking was at evening hours, For then he lost his fear; But most before approaching showers, Or when a storm drew near. Eight years and five round-rolling moons He thus saw steal away, Dozing out all his idle noons, And every night at play. I kept him for his humor’s sake, For he would oft beguile My heart of thoughts that made it ache, And force me to a smile. But now, beneath this walnut-shade He finds his long, last home, And waits in snug concealment laid, Till gentler Puss shall come. He, still more agèd, feels the shocks From which no care can save, And, partner once of Tiney’s box, Must soon partake his grave.

outputs.L2:
Beneath this spot rests old Tiney, the most ill-tempered of his species. No hunting dog ever chased him, no racing greyhound followed his trail; his feet never touched the dawn’s dew, and he never heard a hunter’s cry. Though lovingly raised and kept within domestic boundaries, he remained untamed—a true wild jack-hare.

Each evening he accepted a small allowance of food from my hand, but always watched me suspiciously and bit whenever the chance arose. He ate wheat bread, milk, oats, straw, thistles, and lettuce, along with sand to cleanse his stomach. He also enjoyed hawthorn shoots and the russet skins of apples; when fresh greens were unavailable, sliced carrots satisfied him.

A Turkish carpet served as his meadow. There he delighted in leaping, skipping, and playing like a young deer, twisting his hindquarters as he moved. He became lively after sunset, when his fear subsided, and was especially playful just before rain or as a storm approached.

For eight years and five months he lived this way, sleeping through his uneventful afternoons and spending his nights in play. I kept him because his odd character often distracted me from painful thoughts and made me smile.

Now he lies in his final resting place beneath the shade of a walnut tree, hidden comfortably while he awaits the arrival of the gentler Puss. Puss, older still, is suffering the blows of age that no amount of care can prevent. Once Tiney’s companion in their shared box, he too will soon share this grave.
outputs.L3:
Old Tiney was a domesticated jack-hare, though years of gentle treatment never entirely softened his nature. Despite the tender care he received, he remained surly and wary, always inclined to distrust those around him and sometimes prone to biting.

His diet was remarkably varied. He ate bread and milk, oats and straw, along with thistles, lettuce, hawthorn twigs, apple peel, and carrots. In the evenings, he was allowed to exercise on a Turkey carpet, where he bounded and gambolled with great energy. His liveliness was especially noticeable before rain or an approaching storm, as though he could sense the change in the weather.

For more than eight years, Tiney’s curious habits and amusing behavior brought comfort to his owner. His playful movements helped ease painful thoughts and often inspired smiles during times of sadness. Now Tiney lies buried beneath a walnut tree. In time, it is expected that his elderly companion, Puss, will be laid to rest beside him.
outputs.L4:
The poem serves as an affectionate memorial to Tiney, a jack-hare who spent more than eight years in domestic captivity. Unlike hares pursued by hounds or startled by a hunter’s call, Tiney lived safely within his keeper’s home. Yet comfort and protection never made him truly tame. Even after years of careful nursing, he remained suspicious and surly, accepting his nightly portion of food with a jealous look and sometimes attempting to bite the hand that fed him.

The speaker recalls Tiney’s diet in loving detail. He ate bread, milk, oats, straw, thistles, lettuce, hawthorn twigs, apple peel, and sliced carrots, along with sand to aid his digestion. His indoor world included a Turkey carpet that served as his lawn. There he would bound, skip, gambol, and swing his body around, behaving with the energy of a wild creature despite his confined surroundings. He was especially playful in the evenings, when his fear diminished, and often became livelier before rain or an approaching storm.

For eight years and five months, Tiney passed his days sleeping and his nights in activity. His keeper valued him not because he was gentle or obedient, but because his odd temperament and playful behavior offered emotional relief. Tiney could distract the speaker from painful thoughts, easing an aching heart and compelling him to smile. His companionship therefore had a significance far greater than his stubborn disposition might suggest.

Now Tiney lies buried beneath the shade of a walnut tree. The poem closes by turning to Puss, his gentler and even older companion, who once shared Tiney’s enclosure. Age is already bringing Puss sufferings that no amount of tenderness can prevent, and the speaker knows that he will soon join Tiney in the same grave. The memorial is consequently both humorous and sorrowful: it celebrates the peculiar life of an untamable pet while acknowledging that affection and devoted care, however comforting, cannot protect any living creature from death.
